steps.text: You know eigenvalues and eigenvectors from linear algebra: \(Av = \lambda v\) with \(v \neq 0\). They appear in many applications:
steps.explanation:
• Vibrations: the natural frequencies of a bridge or a building are eigenvalues. If an external excitation (wind, footsteps) matches a natural frequency, resonance threatens.
• Google PageRank: the importance of all web pages is the eigenvector for the largest eigenvalue of a huge matrix.
• Stability: whether a system (e.g. a differential equation) comes to rest or explodes is decided by the eigenvalues.
• Data analysis: principal component analysis looks for eigenvectors of a covariance matrix.

The matrices are often huge – thousands or billions of rows.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Why not just the characteristic polynomial?
steps.insight: Eigenvalues are everywhere – and the matrices are often huge.

steps.text: In linear algebra eigenvalues are computed via the characteristic polynomial. For our example throughout the lesson:
steps.explanation:
Eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = 3\) and \(\lambda_2 = 1\), eigenvectors \(v_1 = (1, 1)\) and \(v_2 = (1, -1)\).

Check: \(A v_1 = (2 + 1,\ 1 + 2) = (3, 3) = 3 v_1\) ✓, \(A v_2 = (2 - 1,\ 1 - 2) = (1, -1) = 1 \cdot v_2\) ✓

For \(2 \times 2\) this is perfect. Why doesn't the computer do the same for large matrices?
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Why not just the characteristic polynomial?
steps.insight: Our example: \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) with eigenvalues 3 and 1.

steps.text: Three reasons why the characteristic polynomial is unsuitable for numerical work:
steps.explanation:
1. No formula: for polynomials of degree 5 and higher there is no general formula for the roots (Abel's theorem). The roots would have to be found numerically anyway.

2. Cost: computing the coefficients of the polynomial from the determinant is expensive for large \(n\).

3. Ill-conditioning: the roots of a polynomial often react extremely sensitively to the smallest changes in the coefficients. Famous example (Wilkinson): the polynomial with roots \(1, 2, \ldots, 20\). Changing one coefficient by \(2^{-23} \approx 10^{-7}\) makes several roots complex – some move by more than \(2\).

The eigenvalues themselves, however, are often well-conditioned (for symmetric matrices always). The detour via the polynomial spoils an actually benign problem – a classic unstable algorithm.

Our roadmap: enclose eigenvalues (Gershgorin), compute one eigenvalue (power method, inverse iteration, Rayleigh quotient), compute all eigenvalues (QR algorithm).
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Why not just the characteristic polynomial?
steps.insight: The characteristic polynomial is an unstable detour. Numerical methods work directly with the matrix.

steps.text: Before computing, you want to know roughly where the eigenvalues are. Gershgorin's theorem provides this with almost no computation:
steps.formula: \text{Every eigenvalue lies in at least one disc } K_i = \Big\{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |z - a_{ii}| \le r_i \Big\}, \quad r_i = \sum_{j \neq i} |a_{ij}|
steps.explanation:
For each row draw a disc in the complex plane:
• Centre: the diagonal element \(a_{ii}\)
• Radius: the sum of the magnitudes of the other entries of the row

All eigenvalues lie in the union of these discs.

For our \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\): both discs have centre \(2\) and radius \(1\). So the eigenvalues lie in \([1, 3]\) – in fact they are exactly \(1\) and \(3\), on the boundary of the disc.
steps.insight: Gershgorin discs: centre \(a_{ii}\), radius = sum of the magnitudes of the rest of the row.

steps.text: Why is that true? The proof is surprisingly short.
steps.explanation:
Let \(Av = \lambda v\), and let \(v_i\) be the component of \(v\) with the largest magnitude. Row \(i\) of \(Av = \lambda v\) reads:
\(\sum_j a_{ij} v_j = \lambda v_i \;\Rightarrow\; (\lambda - a_{ii})\,v_i = \sum_{j \neq i} a_{ij} v_j\)

Take absolute values and divide by \(|v_i|\) (all \(\frac{|v_j|}{|v_i|} \le 1\)):
\(|\lambda - a_{ii}| \le \sum_{j \neq i} |a_{ij}| \frac{|v_j|}{|v_i|} \le \sum_{j \neq i} |a_{ij}| = r_i\)

So \(\lambda\) lies in the disc \(K_i\) – namely the disc belonging to the largest component of the eigenvector.
steps.insight: Proof idea: the row of the largest eigenvector component provides the disc.

steps.text: A \(3 \times 3\) example:
steps.explanation:
The three discs:
• Row 1: centre \(2\), radius \(|1| + |0| = 1\)
• Row 2: centre \(2\), radius \(|-1| + |1| = 2\)
• Row 3: centre \(4\), radius \(|0| + |-1| = 1\)

The animation draws the discs one after another in the complex plane. The actual eigenvalues \(3.54\) and \(2.23 \pm 1.12\,i\) all lie in the union of the discs.

Since the matrix is not symmetric, the eigenvalues may be complex – hence discs and not just intervals.
steps.insight: Gershgorin gives, within seconds, a region in which all eigenvalues must lie.

steps.text: Two useful consequences:
steps.explanation:
• Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues. Then the discs shrink to intervals on the real axis: \([a_{ii} - r_i,\ a_{ii} + r_i]\).

• Invertibility: if \(0\) lies in no disc, \(0\) is not an eigenvalue, so \(A\) is invertible. That is exactly the case when \(|a_{ii}| > r_i\) for all rows – i.e. strict diagonal dominance! So the theorem from “Iterative Solvers for Linear Systems” comes almost for free.

There is also a refinement: if \(k\) discs form a connected group separated from the others, that group contains exactly \(k\) eigenvalues. In the example discs 1 and 2 lie inside each other, and disc 3 overlaps disc 2 – all three form one group.
steps.insight: Strictly diagonally dominant ⇒ 0 lies in no Gershgorin disc ⇒ \(A\) invertible.

steps.text: Quick check: what does Gershgorin say about the eigenvalues of
steps.explanation:
\(B\) is symmetric, so all eigenvalues are real. The intervals:
• Row 1: \([10 - 1,\ 10 + 1] = [9, 11]\)
• Row 2: \([5 - 2,\ 5 + 2] = [3, 7]\)
• Row 3: \([1 - 1,\ 1 + 1] = [0, 2]\)

The three intervals are separate, so each contains exactly one eigenvalue. Without any computation we know: one eigenvalue between 9 and 11, one between 3 and 7, one between 0 and 2.

Is \(B\) invertible? The lowest interval contains \(0\) at its edge – Gershgorin alone does not decide this here.
steps.insight: Separate Gershgorin discs contain exactly one eigenvalue each.

steps.text: Now the simplest method for actually computing an eigenvalue: the power method (vector iteration). The idea is astonishingly simple – multiply a starting vector by \(A\) again and again:
steps.formula: x_0, \quad A x_0, \quad A^2 x_0, \quad A^3 x_0, \quad \ldots
steps.explanation:
With \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(x_0 = (1, 0)\):
• \(A x_0 = (2, 1)\)
• \(A^2 x_0 = A(2, 1) = (5, 4)\)
• \(A^3 x_0 = (14, 13)\)
• \(A^4 x_0 = (41, 40)\)

The two components become more and more alike – the vector turns towards \((1, 1)\), the eigenvector for the largest eigenvalue \(3\).
steps.insight: Power method: multiply by \(A\) again and again. The direction approaches the dominant eigenvector.

steps.text: Why does this work? Decompose the starting vector into eigenvectors:
steps.explanation:
Each multiplication by \(A\) multiplies the \(v_1\) part by \(3\) and the \(v_2\) part by \(1\). After \(k\) steps the \(v_1\) part has grown \(3^k\) times as much.

Check for \(k = 3\): \(\frac{27}{2}(1, 1) + \frac{1}{2}(1, -1) = (13.5 + 0.5,\ 13.5 - 0.5) = (14, 13)\) ✓

The eigenvector for the eigenvalue of largest magnitude “wins” – it is called the dominant eigenvector. The animation shows how the direction of the iterates approaches the eigenline.
steps.insight: The part along the dominant eigenvector grows fastest and takes over.

steps.text: A practical problem: the numbers grow like \(3^k\). After 1000 steps that would be \(3^{1000}\) – overflow! That is why one normalises in every step:
steps.explanation:
The direction stays the same, only the length is set to \(1\). Any norm will do. By hand the \(\infty\)-norm is most convenient (divide by the component of largest magnitude).

Our iteration with this normalisation:
\(\begin{array}{c|c|c} k & y_k = A x_{k-1} & x_k \\ \hline 1 & (2,\ 1) & (1,\ 0.5) \\ 2 & (2.5,\ 2) & (1,\ 0.8) \\ 3 & (2.8,\ 2.6) & (1,\ 0.929) \\ 4 & (2.929,\ 2.857) & (1,\ 0.976) \\ 5 & (2.976,\ 2.951) & (1,\ 0.992) \end{array}\)

The number we divide by (\(2,\ 2.5,\ 2.8,\ 2.93,\ 2.98\)) approaches the eigenvalue \(3\).
steps.insight: Normalise in every step. The normalisation factor converges to \(|\lambda_1|\).

steps.text: How fast does this go? Relative to the dominant part, the disturbing part shrinks in every step by the factor
steps.explanation:
\(\lambda_1\) is the eigenvalue of largest magnitude, \(\lambda_2\) the second largest.

In the example: \(q = \frac{1}{3}\). The errors of the eigenvalue estimate: \(1,\ 0.5,\ 0.2,\ 0.07,\ 0.024, \ldots\) – each about a third. Linear convergence.

If the two largest eigenvalues are close together (e.g. \(\lambda_1 = 10\), \(\lambda_2 = 9.9\)), then \(q = 0.99\) – and hundreds of steps are needed for a few digits.
steps.insight: Convergence factor of the power method: \(|\lambda_2 / \lambda_1|\). Close eigenvalues ⇒ slow.

steps.text: When does the power method fail?
steps.explanation:
• Two dominant eigenvalues of equal magnitude, e.g. \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) with eigenvalues \(1\) and \(-1\). From \(x_0 = (1, 0)\): \((0, 1),\ (1, 0),\ (0, 1), \ldots\) – the iteration jumps back and forth and never converges.

• Complex dominant eigenvalues (\(\lambda = a \pm bi\), same magnitude): the iterates rotate in circles.

• Starting vector without a component along the dominant eigenvector: with \(x_0 = (1, -1) = v_2\) you stay at \(v_2\) forever. In practice this is no problem – rounding errors almost always create a small component along \(v_1\), which then grows. Still, one usually starts with a random vector.
steps.insight: The power method needs a unique eigenvalue of largest magnitude.

steps.text: A famous application: Google's PageRank.
steps.explanation:
Imagine a surfer who follows links at random. The matrix \(G\) contains the transition probabilities between all web pages. The importance of the pages is the vector \(x\) with \(Gx = x\) – the eigenvector for the eigenvalue \(1\), which is the largest here.

The matrix has billions of rows, but each page has only a few links – it is extremely sparse. A multiplication \(Gx\) is therefore cheap.

Google originally computed PageRank with exactly the power method. Thanks to a “damping factor” of \(0.85\) (the surfer sometimes jumps to a random page) \(|\lambda_2| \le 0.85\), and about 50 to 100 iterations suffice.
steps.insight: The power method needs only matrix–vector products – ideal for huge sparse matrices.

steps.text: How do you best estimate the eigenvalue from an approximate vector \(x\)? The best choice is the Rayleigh quotient:
steps.explanation:
If \(x\) is an exact eigenvector, then \(x^{T}Ax = x^{T}(\lambda x) = \lambda\,x^{T}x\), so \(r(x) = \lambda\) ✓

For approximations, \(r(x)\) is the value \(\lambda\) that minimises \(\|Ax - \lambda x\|\) – in the least squares sense the best eigenvalue for \(x\).

Example \(x = (2, 1)\): \(Ax = (5, 4)\), \(x^{T}Ax = 10 + 4 = 14\), \(x^{T}x = 5\), so \(r = 2.8\).
steps.insight: Rayleigh quotient \(r(x) = \frac{x^{T}Ax}{x^{T}x}\): the best eigenvalue estimate for a vector \(x\).

steps.text: For symmetric matrices the Rayleigh quotient is particularly accurate. Comparison for the iterates of the power method:
steps.explanation:
The error of the direction (component along \(v_2\) relative to \(v_1\)) drops by the factor \(\frac{1}{3}\) per step. The error of the Rayleigh quotient drops by the factor \(\frac{1}{9} = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\)!

The reason: for symmetric \(A\), \(|r(x) - \lambda| \approx C \cdot (\text{angle error})^2\). A vector with 3 correct digits gives an eigenvalue with about 6 correct digits.
steps.insight: For symmetric matrices the error of the Rayleigh quotient is roughly the square of the vector error.

steps.text: Quick check: compute the Rayleigh quotient of \(x = (1, 1)\) and \(x = (1, 2)\) for \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\).
steps.explanation:
• \(x = (1, 1)\): \(Ax = (3, 3)\), \(r = \frac{3 + 3}{2} = 3\) – exact, because \((1, 1)\) is an eigenvector.

• \(x = (1, 2)\): \(Ax = (4, 5)\), \(x^{T}Ax = 4 + 10 = 14\), \(x^{T}x = 5\), \(r = 2.8\).

The vector \((1, 2)\) is quite far from the eigenvector (angle about \(18°\)), yet \(r = 2.8\) is already close to \(3\).

In general, for symmetric \(A\): \(\lambda_{\min} \le r(x) \le \lambda_{\max}\) for every \(x \neq 0\).
steps.insight: The Rayleigh quotient always lies between the smallest and largest eigenvalue (for symmetric matrices).

steps.text: The power method finds only the eigenvalue of largest magnitude. What about the smallest? Trick: the inverse matrix has the reciprocals as eigenvalues.
steps.explanation:
The smallest eigenvalue of \(A\) (in magnitude) becomes the largest of \(A^{-1}\). So one applies the power method to \(A^{-1}\): inverse iteration.

But careful: \(A^{-1}\) is never computed explicitly! Instead of \(y_k = A^{-1}x_{k-1}\) one solves the linear system
\(A\,y_k = x_{k-1}\)

It is best to compute the LU decomposition of \(A\) once and then solve only two triangular systems in each step (\(O(n^2)\)).
steps.insight: Inverse iteration: power method with \(A^{-1}\) – solve a linear system in each step, do not invert.

steps.text: Even more powerful is the shift: take an estimate \(\mu\) and iterate with \((A - \mu I)^{-1}\).
steps.explanation:
The eigenvalue closest to \(\mu\) gives the largest value \(\frac{1}{|\lambda - \mu|}\) and takes over.

So you can find any eigenvalue if you have a good estimate – for example from Gershgorin.

Convergence factor: \(\frac{|\lambda_{\text{closest}} - \mu|}{|\lambda_{\text{second closest}} - \mu|}\). The closer \(\mu\) is to the desired eigenvalue, the faster.
steps.insight: Inverse iteration with shift \(\mu\): finds the eigenvalue closest to \(\mu\).

steps.text: Example: we look for the eigenvalue of \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) near \(\mu = 0.9\).
steps.explanation:
The eigenvalues of \((A - 0.9I)^{-1}\) are \(\frac{1}{2.1} \approx 0.48\) and \(\frac{1}{0.1} = 10\). Convergence factor: \(\frac{0.48}{10} \approx 0.048\) – very fast!

Iteration from \((1, 0)\), normalised each time, with Rayleigh quotient:
\(\begin{array}{c|c|c} k & x_k & r(x_k) \\ \hline 1 & (1,\ -0.909) & 1.0045 \\ 2 & (1,\ -0.9955) & 1.00001 \\ 3 & (1,\ -0.99978) & 1.00000002 \end{array}\)

After three steps: eigenvalue \(1\) to 8 digits, eigenvector almost exactly \((1, -1)\).
steps.insight: A good shift makes inverse iteration extremely fast.

steps.text: The crowning touch: adapt the shift in every step and take the current Rayleigh quotient. This is Rayleigh quotient iteration:
steps.explanation:
Since the shift keeps improving, convergence also becomes faster and faster. For symmetric matrices it is cubic: the number of correct digits triples in each step (\(10^{-2} \to 10^{-6} \to 10^{-18}\)).

The price: since the shift changes, a new LU decomposition is needed in each step (\(O(n^3)\)). And you do not know in advance exactly which eigenvalue you will end up at.

Important note: \(A - \mu I\) is almost singular when \(\mu\) is almost an eigenvalue. Exceptionally, this is wanted here – the error in solving points exactly in the direction of the desired eigenvector.
steps.insight: Rayleigh quotient iteration: shift = current Rayleigh quotient. Cubic convergence for symmetric matrices.

steps.text: Quick check: by Gershgorin a symmetric matrix has eigenvalues in \([9, 11]\), \([3, 7]\) and \([0, 2]\). Which method and which starting value find the middle eigenvalue?
steps.explanation:
The power method would find the largest (in the interval \([9, 11]\)), inverse iteration without shift the smallest (in \([0, 2]\)).

For the middle one: inverse iteration with a shift, for example \(\mu = 5\) (middle of the middle interval). The middle eigenvalue is at most \(2\) away from \(5\), the others at least \(3\). So the convergence factor is at most \(\frac{2}{3}\).

Even faster: after a few steps switch to Rayleigh quotient iteration.
steps.insight: Gershgorin provides good shifts for inverse iteration.

steps.text: Often all eigenvalues of a matrix are needed. The standard method for that is the QR algorithm – one of the most important methods of the 20th century. Its basic form is astonishingly simple:
steps.formula: A_0 = A, \qquad A_k = Q_k R_k \;\text{(QR decomposition)}, \qquad A_{k+1} = R_k Q_k
steps.explanation:
Decompose \(A_k\) into \(Q_k R_k\) (see “Least Squares & QR Decomposition”) and multiply the factors back together in reverse order.

Why does this not change the eigenvalues? Because \(R_k = Q_k^{T} A_k\):
\(A_{k+1} = R_k Q_k = Q_k^{T} A_k Q_k\)

That is a similarity transformation with an orthogonal matrix. Similar matrices have the same eigenvalues. And since \(Q_k\) is orthogonal, rounding errors are not amplified.
steps.insight: QR algorithm: decompose \(A_k = Q_kR_k\), multiply in reverse \(A_{k+1} = R_kQ_k\). The eigenvalues stay the same.

steps.text: One QR step for \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) (with Gram–Schmidt):
steps.explanation:
Check of the trace (sum of the diagonal = sum of the eigenvalues): \(2.8 + 1.2 = 4 = 3 + 1\) ✓

The diagonal has changed from \((2, 2)\) to \((2.8, 1.2)\) – towards the eigenvalues \((3, 1)\). The off-diagonal has shrunk from \(1\) to \(0.6\).

Remarkably, \(2.8\) is exactly the Rayleigh quotient from the power method. The QR algorithm secretly performs a power method – for all eigenvalues at once.
steps.insight: One QR step moves the diagonal towards the eigenvalues and shrinks the entries outside it.

steps.text: Further QR steps:
steps.explanation:
The off-diagonal shrinks by the factor \(\frac{1}{3} = \frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\) per step. The diagonal converges to the eigenvalues \(3\) and \(1\).

In general \(A_k\) converges to an upper triangular matrix (for symmetric matrices to a diagonal matrix). All eigenvalues are then on the diagonal, ordered by size.

The convergence factor for the entry \((i+1, i)\) is \(\left|\frac{\lambda_{i+1}}{\lambda_i}\right|\) – as in the power method.
steps.insight: The QR algorithm converges to a triangular matrix with the eigenvalues on the diagonal.

steps.text: The basic form is still too slow and too expensive. Professional implementations (for example behind eig in MATLAB or NumPy) use three improvements:
steps.explanation:
• Hessenberg form: first bring \(A\) to Hessenberg form with Householder reflections (zeros below the first subdiagonal; tridiagonal for symmetric matrices). A QR step then costs only \(O(n^2)\) instead of \(O(n^3)\).

• Shifts: as in inverse iteration, decompose \(A_k - \mu_k I\) instead of \(A_k\). With good shifts the last row converges quadratically or even cubically.

• Deflation: once an off-diagonal entry is small enough, the matrix is split into two smaller parts and the work continues with these.

Together, all eigenvalues of an \(n \times n\) matrix take about \(10n^3\) operations. For \(n = 1000\) that is done in a second.
steps.insight: In practice: Hessenberg form + shifts + deflation make the QR algorithm fast and reliable.

steps.text: Quick check: which method for which task?
steps.explanation:
• Rough location of all eigenvalues, without computing: Gershgorin.
• Only the eigenvalue of largest magnitude of a huge sparse matrix (e.g. PageRank): power method.
• One particular eigenvalue for which you have an estimate: inverse iteration with shift or Rayleigh quotient iteration.
• All eigenvalues of a medium-sized dense matrix: QR algorithm (eig).
• Some eigenvalues of a huge sparse matrix: Krylov methods such as Lanczos or Arnoldi (a further development of the power method, not part of this lesson).
steps.insight: Gershgorin to enclose, power method/inverse iteration for single eigenvalues, QR for all.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. The characteristic polynomial is a bad numerical route (no formula from degree 5, ill-conditioned roots).

2. Gershgorin: all eigenvalues lie in the discs around \(a_{ii}\) with radius \(\sum_{j \neq i}|a_{ij}|\).

3. Power method: \(x_k = \frac{Ax_{k-1}}{\|Ax_{k-1}\|}\) converges to the dominant eigenvector, factor \(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|\).

4. Rayleigh quotient \(r(x) = \frac{x^{T}Ax}{x^{T}x}\): best eigenvalue estimate, with quadratically small error for symmetric matrices.

5. Inverse iteration with shift \(\mu\): solve \((A - \mu I)y = x\), finds the eigenvalue near \(\mu\). Rayleigh quotient iteration: cubic.

6. QR algorithm: \(A_k = Q_kR_k\), \(A_{k+1} = R_kQ_k\) – similarity transformations, convergence to triangular form. In practice with Hessenberg form, shifts and deflation.
steps.insight: Key message: eigenvalues are computed iteratively and directly from the matrix – never via the characteristic polynomial.

steps.text: What comes next? Eigenvalues play a leading role in the next two lessons.
steps.explanation:
In “One-Step Methods for ODEs” you will learn how to solve differential equations such as \(y' = \lambda y\) numerically step by step.

In “Stiff ODEs & Multistep Methods” it then becomes decisive where the eigenvalues of the system matrix lie: if they differ greatly in size, the system is “stiff”, and explicit methods explode – exactly when the value \(h\lambda\) falls outside a certain region of the complex plane. The complex plane you saw with Gershgorin becomes important again there.
steps.insight: Next block: differential equations – and there eigenvalues decide stability.
